summaries.example: Imagine a path in a park that splits into two trails. Before the split, both trails share the same path. After the split, one trail might lead to a pond and the other to a playground. A branching-time picture uses this idea for possible events: the shared path is the past, and the trails are different possible futures.
summaries.summary: Branching time is a way to represent a system’s possible developments. The system might be the whole universe, a computer program, or something else. In the usual picture, moments are connected into histories. A history is one complete possible way events could go. Several histories may overlap for a while and then branch into different futures. Standard branching-time trees allow forward branching but not backward branching: two possible futures may share one past, while one moment does not have two different pasts within the model. These structures are useful in logic, where they help explain statements about the past, future, and possibility. They are also used in computer science to represent different possible executions of a program. Some philosophers think a tree is more than a useful diagram: they think reality itself may have a branching structure. Others think trees are only tools for describing possibilities, or prefer structures in which possible histories are kept separate. The entry presents these views and the disagreements among them without treating one as settled.
key_ideas: Branching-time models show several possible futures that share some earlier events.
In standard trees, the future can split, but two different pasts do not join into one past.
Philosophers use these models to think about choices, open futures, and statements about what will happen.
Different models can represent possibilities in different ways; no single interpretation is accepted by everyone.
Related ideas are used in computer science to describe the possible runs of a program.
summaries.why_it_matters: Branching time gives us a careful way to talk about an open future. It helps separate what is possible now from what was possible earlier, and it shows why “could happen” may depend on when we ask. The same ideas help logicians study future statements and help computer scientists check whether programs behave safely along all their possible runs. Studying the model also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a simple-looking picture can support several different ideas about time, reality, and possibility.

important_terms.definition: A picture or mathematical structure showing different possible ways events might unfold over time.
A complete possible course of events, from earlier moments through later ones.
A very small time-slice or event in a branching-time picture.
A point where one shared course can continue in different ways.

questions_to_think_about: If two futures are possible now, does one of them become the real future later?
Can two different histories share the same past but separate after a choice?
Is a computer program with two possible next steps like a branching-time tree?
Should a picture of possibilities show every possible path, or only the paths we are studying?

summaries.example: Suppose a program reaches state s0 and can next enter either s1 or s2. From s1 it may continue through one sequence of states, while from s2 it follows another. A branching-time model treats each complete execution as a history. A statement such as “the program will eventually reach an error state” can then be interpreted in different ways: it may hold on one selected execution, on every execution still open from s0, or on at least one execution. These correspond to different semantic treatments of the future.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents branching time (BT) as a label for three related projects: formal structures, semantics for tense-modal logics, and metaphysical conceptions of time and modality. The central structure is a tree whose nodes are moments and whose maximal ordered paths are histories. Histories represent complete possible developments, while shared initial segments represent events common to several possibilities. Standard BT trees impose connection and no backward branching. Thus, possible futures may diverge, but the past of a moment remains linear. This is intended to capture historical, objective possibility rather than mere uncertainty caused by incomplete knowledge. The entry compares trees with bundled trees, in which only selected histories count as admissible, and with non-branching representations such as Kamp and Ockhamist frames, where histories are initially represented as separate worlds and their overlap is encoded by additional relations. Branching Space-Times (BST) modifies the basic picture for relativity: its primitive entities are point events ordered by causal precedence, and histories need not be linearly ordered because spacelike separated events can be incomparable. In logic, recursive approaches include thin-red-line, Peircean, and Ockhamist semantics. Postsemantic approaches, including supervaluationism and relativism, address the difficulty of assigning truth to ordinary future-tense assertions when the present belongs to several histories. The metaphysical debate includes branching-time realism, actual futurism, and asymmetry views. The entry stresses that links between a semantic theory and a metaphysical theory are natural connections, not entailments. key_ideas: Standard BT frames are trees of moments and histories. Their structural conditions include connection and no backward branching.
Historical modality is time-sensitive: a future may be open at one moment but no longer open after an event has occurred.
Different semantics interpret future claims differently. Ockhamist semantics uses a moment-history pair, while Peircean and supervaluationist approaches quantify over histories in other ways.
A semantic framework does not logically force a particular metaphysical view. The same tree can be used by philosophers with different commitments about actuality, time, and existence.

The distinction between forward branching and backward branching matters. Supporters of no backward branching emphasize particular events and objective historical possibility; critics question whether physics supports such a temporal asymmetry.
Branching Space-Times replaces idealized world-slices with point events and causal order, allowing relativity and indeterminism to be studied together.
summaries.why_it_matters: Branching-time theory connects abstract logic with questions people already ask: what was genuinely possible, whether the future is open, and how a claim about tomorrow can be true or false. It also clarifies how a model represents identity across alternatives and how possibility differs from ignorance. In computer science, related structures support temporal logics for describing and verifying programs. In philosophy of physics, Branching Space-Times explores whether indeterminism can be represented without assuming a Newtonian, globally synchronized picture. important_terms.definition: A family of structures, logical interpretations, and metaphysical views used to represent multiple possible temporal developments.
A maximal, linearly ordered chain of moments representing a complete possible course of events.
An abstract node representing an instantaneous or minimally extended event or world-slice.
The condition that a model has a single connected structure rather than unrelated components.
The condition that the past of each moment is linearly ordered, so standard trees branch toward the future but not toward the past.
A semantics that evaluates a formula at a moment together with a history passing through that moment.
A view on which all times are metaphysically on a par, rather than the present having an objective privilege.
A relativistic framework whose basic items are spatially limited point events ordered by causal precedence.

Does representing all possible futures make them equally real, or can the tree remain merely a useful model?
Why might objective historical possibility differ from what an agent merely does not know?
Could a model allow both forward and backward branching without confusing alternative events with alternative information?

summaries.example: A school robotics program has reached the same setup in every possible run. From that setup, a sensor might detect a wall or might not. The runs now split. One history includes a turn; another includes moving straight ahead. If we ask before the sensor result, both futures are open. After the result, the history in which the other result occurred may no longer be a live historical possibility from that point. A branching-time diagram represents the shared setup as one moment and the different runs as branches.
summaries.summary: Branching time is both a formal model and a family of philosophical views about time and possibility. In the standard model, moments are connected by a temporal order, and a history is a complete possible path through them. Histories can coincide over an earlier stretch and then divide. The model therefore represents indeterminism as forward branching. It normally excludes backward branching, meaning that the past of any moment is ordered as one line rather than as several incompatible pasts joining together. This restriction is meant to concern concrete, non-repeatable events and objective historical possibility, not the many things an observer might be unable to know. The entry examines several ways to represent the same general idea. Bundled trees include only a selected group of admissible histories. Kamp and Ockhamist frames treat histories more like separate worlds and use relations to represent their shared moments. Synchronization can add a way to identify moments on different histories as occurring at the same time, but this introduces substantial assumptions about time. Branching Space-Times develops a related framework for relativity. Its basic units are point events, ordered by causal precedence, rather than entire instantaneous universe-slices. In logical applications, future operators can be interpreted in competing ways. A thin-red-line view selects an actual future, Peircean semantics treats a future event as future only when it is unavoidable, and Ockhamist semantics evaluates claims relative to a chosen history. Postsemantic theories try to explain ordinary assertions made before a future is settled, sometimes by making truth depend on the context from which the claim is assessed. key_ideas: Branching-time trees distinguish a shared past from multiple possible futures.
The phrase “it was possible” is incomplete unless we ask when it was possible; possibilities can change as events occur.
Standard trees concern objective possibilities of particular events, not simply possibilities compatible with someone’s limited information.
Philosophers disagree about whether all branches are equally real, whether one future is privileged, or whether future branches are abstract possibilities.
Logical systems differ over how to interpret future statements: some select a history, some require truth across histories, and some allow a future statement to lack a settled truth value.
Computer scientists use related branching structures to represent different executions of the same program.
summaries.why_it_matters: Branching time helps explain why “possible” is not a single, context-free idea. A move may be possible before a decision and impossible afterward, even though it remains logically imaginable. The framework also reveals how views about time affect language: whether a future claim is true, false, or unsettled may depend on whether we evaluate one history or all histories. In computer science, the same pattern appears when a program can execute along several paths and we ask whether a property holds on every path. Studying the disagreements helps readers see how formal models can illuminate philosophical questions without settling them by themselves.

important_terms.definition: A model of several possible ways a system can develop through time, with some developments sharing earlier moments.
One complete possible route through a branching-time model.
A node standing for an instantaneous or minimally extended event in the model.
A possible future continuing from a particular moment along one history.
A kind of possibility tied to a particular time and to what can still happen from there, rather than to mere lack of knowledge.
The rule in standard trees that alternatives may separate toward the future but do not combine into different pasts.
A logical method that evaluates a future claim relative to a moment and a history passing through it.
A representation designed to combine indeterminism with the causal structure emphasized by relativity.

questions_to_think_about: If a possibility disappears after an event, was it ever a real possibility or only a possibility based on incomplete information?
Would a tree be a picture of reality, or only a convenient representation of what could happen?
Why might a philosopher want histories to overlap rather than exist as completely separate worlds?
How does evaluating a statement on one history differ from evaluating it on every history?
What might relativity change about the idea that a moment is a complete slice of the entire universe?
